jl-01.title: The Three Japanese Scripts
explain: **Japanese** mixes three kinds of script within a single sentence: **hiragana**, **katakana**, and **kanji**. It looks complicated at first, but each script has its own job, so once your eye gets used to them they become cues for where to break a sentence. This lesson gives a big-picture view of what each script does.

**Hiragana** has many round, soft curves. It is a script that represents sounds (a **phonetic script**), with 46 basic characters. It is used to write **particles** (short words such as は and を), the endings of verbs and adjectives, and everyday native words.

**Katakana** has many straight lines and angles. It has the same sounds as hiragana and differs only in shape. It is mainly used to write words that came from abroad (**loanwords**), the names of foreign people and countries, and words that imitate sounds, and it is sometimes used to emphasize a word.

**Kanji** are characters that originally came from China, and each character represents a meaning (an **ideographic script**). In 日本, 日 means sun and 本 means origin or book. Some kanji used in Japan are the same as Korean hanja, but others have simpler shapes, such as 学 (Korean 學). Many kanji have more than one reading. Reading a kanji by fitting it to a native Japanese word is called the **kun reading**, and a reading that comes from Chinese-style pronunciation is called the **on reading**. 山 is read やま (yama) in the kun reading and さん (san) in the on reading.

explain.alt: The sentence 「私はコーヒーを飲みます」 is divided into eleven boxes. Under each box is a Korean label: 한 for kanji, 히 for hiragana, or 가 for katakana. In order: 私 (한, kanji), は (히, hiragana), the four boxes of コーヒー (가, katakana), を (히), 飲 (한), and the three boxes み, ま, す (히). Below is 'Meaning: I drink coffee' (written in Korean) and a legend.
explain.caption: The three scripts in one sentence (an original example)

explain: As in the figure, a sentence usually has kanji (私, 飲) anchoring the meaning, hiragana (は, を, みます) connecting the grammar, and katakana (コーヒー) handling the loanword. The places where the script changes are often where words break, which is a great help when reading Japanese, which has no spaces.

Text is generally written horizontally. Some writing, such as novels and newspapers, runs vertically. A sentence ends with the period 「。」, and a pause for reading is marked with 「、」. Ordinary text puts no spaces between words. In this course, to make reading easier for beginners, we sometimes deliberately add spaces.

examples.title: Writing one word in three scripts
body: The word meaning cat can be written 猫 in kanji, ねこ in hiragana, and ネコ in katakana. The sound is neko in all three. A writer chooses the script to suit the reader, the mood, and the kind of text.
In everyday writing ねこ is used casually, and ネコ is sometimes used when one wants to make clear that it is the animal, or when writing in the style of a field guide.

jl-02.title: Hiragana and the Gojūon Chart
explain: Hiragana is a script that represents sounds. The chart that collects the basic characters is called the **gojūon chart** (the "fifty-sound chart"). Although the name contains the number fifty, the number of characters now in use is 46. In the chart, a horizontal line is called a **row** (a consonant series) and a vertical line is called a **column** (a vowel series). The figure below is the chart laid on its side. From the top the rows are the vowel row (a), the k row, the s row, and so on, and the columns run in the order a, i, u, e, o.

explain.alt: A gojūon chart. The rows, from the top, are -, k, s, t, n, h, m, y, r, w, n, and the columns are a, i, u, e, o. The characters in the cells, from the top, are あいうえお, かきくけこ, さしすせそ, たちつてと, なにぬねの, はひふへほ, まみむめも, や (blank) ゆ (blank) よ, らりるれろ, わ (three blanks) を, and ん. The cells of し, ち, つ, and ふ carry an asterisk, and at the right is written '* marks: し shi, ち chi, つ tsu, ふ fu'.
explain.caption: The hiragana gojūon chart (an original chart)

explain: A blank cell is a place with no character. Cells with no sound are left empty, and in modern Japanese the や row has only three characters, や, ゆ, and よ, and the わ row has only two, わ and を. So the number of cells is 5 × 8 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 46. The final ん takes up a row by itself.

Sounds can only be written **approximately** in Korean. To know the exact sound you have to hear Japanese pronunciation yourself. The vowels are あ (a), い (i), う (close to u, but with the lips less rounded), え (e), and お (o). The か row sounds close to "ka" at the start of a word and sometimes closer to "ga" in the middle of a word. さ is "sa", な is "na", ま is "ma", and the ら row is a sound made by lightly flicking the tip of the tongue once, so it sounds somewhere between "ra" and "da". ん sounds like "n" or "ng" depending on the sound that follows.

The four cells with an asterisk (*) need attention. Rather than the si, ti, tu, hu you would get by spelling in the Roman letters according to the rule, in the Hepburn system し is written shi, ち is chi, つ is tsu (a sound close to "tsu"), and ふ is fu (an "fu" made between the lips). These four sound slightly different from the other characters in their rows.

A dot can also be added to a character to change its sound. Putting two dots at the upper right (the **dakuten**) turns か into が (ga), さ into ざ (za), た into だ (da), and は into ば (ba). The small circle (the **handakuten**) is used only with the は row, turning は into ぱ (pa). The small っ is a mark telling you to double the consonant that follows. In がっこう (school), the k sound is doubled, as in gakkō. The small ゃ, ゅ, and ょ combine with the preceding character to make a single sound. For example, き + ゃ is きゃ (kya).

examples.title: Reading words in hiragana
body: さかな is さ (sa) + か (ka) + な (na), which gives sakana, and means "fish". やま is や (ya) + ま (ma), which gives yama, and means "mountain". みず is み (mi) + ず (zu), which gives mizu, and means "water". You can read a word by finding each character's cell in the chart and joining the sounds.
In the figure, み is in the m row, i column, and ず is the character す (s row, u column) with a dakuten added.

Even for the same character は, with no marks it is ha, with a dakuten it is ba, and with a circle it is pa.

jl-03.title: Katakana and Loanwords
explain: **Katakana** is the counterpart of hiragana. Its cell layout and sounds in the gojūon chart are the same, and only the shapes differ. It has many straight lines and angular shapes, which distinguishes it from the curvy hiragana. The figure below pairs up the first two rows.

explain.alt: Ten cells are arranged in two rows. Each cell has a hiragana on top, a katakana below it, and Roman letters at the bottom. The first row is あ-ア a, い-イ i, う-ウ u, え-エ e, お-オ o, and the second row is か-カ ka, き-キ ki, く-ク ku, け-ケ ke, こ-コ ko.
explain.caption: Hiragana and katakana pairs (an original chart)

explain: Some pairs have similar shapes (カ and か), and some are quite different (あ and ア look somewhat alike, but they have to be learned separately). There are pairs that are especially confusing when you first learn them: シ (shi) and ツ (tsu), and ソ (so) and ン (n). Because the shapes are similar, let us learn them by looking at them together with the characters before and after in a word.

The biggest job of katakana is writing **loanwords**. Many words sound similar to Korean loanwords, such as コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), テレビ (terebi, television), ホテル (hoteru, hotel), バス (basu, bus), ケーキ (kēki, cake), and タクシー (takushī, taxi). The names of foreign countries are also written in katakana, as in アメリカ (the United States), フランス (France), and ドイツ (Germany).

In katakana, 「ー」 is used when lengthening a sound. In コーヒー, ー means to extend the vowel of the preceding character by one more beat. So it becomes a long vowel, as in kōhī. Small ァ, ィ, ゥ, ェ, and ォ are also attached to imitate foreign-language sounds. パーティー (pātī, party) and フォーク (fōku, fork) are examples.

Not every loanword comes from English. パン (pan, bread) is commonly explained as having come from Portuguese. There are also words made in Japan by combining English words. サラリーマン (sarariiman) is a Japanese-made term meaning a company employee who receives a salary. Such words may not be understood as they are by English speakers.

examples.title: Reading katakana words
body: タクシー is タ (ta) + ク (ku) + シ (shi) + ー (lengthening), giving takushī. Its sound resembles the Korean "택시" (taeksi), so it is easy to guess the meaning. バス is バ (ba) + ス (su), giving basu, and means "bus".
テレビ is a word shortened by taking the first and middle parts of "television". Japanese likes to shorten long loanwords.

jl-04.title: Sentence Structure and Particles
explain: It has not been proven that Japanese and Korean belong to the same language family, but the ways they build sentences are very similar. The biggest thing they share is **word order**. The basic order is **subject - object - verb**, and the verb comes at the very end. This differs from English, where "I read a book" has the verb in the middle.

explain.alt: The sentence 「私は 本を 読みます」 is divided into three chunks. Chunk 1 is 私は (わたしは, 저는, subject/topic), chunk 2 is 本を (ほんを, 책을, object), and chunk 3 is 読みます (よみます, 읽습니다, verb). は and を carry a label meaning 'particle'. Below is written, in Korean, 'As in Korean, the verb comes at the very end.' (The Korean glosses 저는, 책을, 읽습니다 mean 'as for me', 'the book (object)', and 'read'.)
explain.caption: The chunks of a basic Japanese sentence (an original example)

explain:
Another point of similarity is the **particle**. A particle attaches after a word and shows what job that word does in the sentence. Japanese has words corresponding to the Korean 은/는 and 을/를. The main particles are as follows.
- **は**: marks the topic of the discussion (corresponding to Korean ~은/는). When used as a particle it is read "wa," not "ha."
- **が**: marks the subject (corresponding to Korean ~이/가). It is often used with words such as "be (there)" and "like."
- **を**: marks the object of an action (corresponding to Korean ~을/를). Its sound is "o."
- **に**: marks the place of arrival, the time, and the place where something exists (roughly "to, at, in"; Korean ~에).
- **で**: marks the place where an action occurs or the means (roughly "at, by, with"; Korean ~에서, ~로).
- **の**: marks possession or belonging (roughly "of"; Korean ~의).

They do not match Korean exactly. は and 은/는, and が and 이/가, correspond for the most part, but they do not always agree. At first it is enough to remember only that "they roughly correspond like this."

Verbs also change their endings, as in Korean. For "read," 読む (よむ) is the dictionary form, and it changes to 読みます (よみます) when speaking politely. In the same way, 行く (いく, go) becomes 行きます (いきます) and 食べる (たべる, eat) becomes 食べます (たべます). ~ます is a polite style similar to the Korean "~ㅂ니다" (-mnida).
A modifier comes before the word it modifies. 大きい猫 (おおきい ねこ) is "a big cat." This too is the same as in Korean.

examples.title: Building sentences with particles
body: 「私は 学校に 行きます」 (わたしは がっこうに いきます) means "I go to school." に shows the destination.
「図書館で 本を 読みます」 (としょかんで ほんを よみます) means "I read a book at the library." で shows the place where the act of reading occurs, and を is attached to the book, the thing being read.

examples.title: Linking with の
body: 「私の 本」 (わたしの ほん) is "my book." の shows that the preceding word (私) is the owner of the following word (本). It comes in the same position as the Korean "의" (ui).
「あそこに 猫が います」 (あそこに ねこが います) means "There is a cat over there." When something alive exists, います is used. に shows the place of existence, and が shows the thing that exists.

jl-05.title: Greetings and Self-Introduction Expressions
explain: This lesson covers the most frequently used greetings and the "is/am ~" sentence pattern. Sounds are given in Roman letters, so remember that they differ from the actual sounds.

explain.alt: Four lines of greetings. Morning: おはようございます (ohayo gozaimasu, morning greeting). Daytime: こんにちは (konnichiwa, daytime greeting). Evening: こんばんは (konbanwa, evening greeting). Thanks: ありがとうございます (arigato gozaimasu, greeting of thanks).
explain.caption: Greetings by time of day (an original example)

explain:
- おはようございます (ohayo gozaimasu, approximate): a morning greeting. Among close friends only おはよう is used.
- こんにちは (konnichiwa, approximate): a greeting used during the day. The final は is read "wa," the same as the particle は.
- こんばんは (konbanwa, approximate): an evening greeting.
- ありがとうございます (arigato gozaimasu, approximate): an expression of thanks.
- すみません (sumimasen, approximate): used to apologize or to get someone's attention, like "I'm sorry" or "Excuse me."
- はじめまして (hajimemashite, approximate): "How do you do? / Nice to meet you."
- よろしくおねがいします (yoroshiku onegai shimasu): "Please treat me well / I look forward to working with you." It is often used at the end of a first meeting.
- いただきます (itadakimasu) / ごちそうさま (gochisōsama): words said before and after a meal.

The core of self-introduction is **~です** (desu). "A is B" is said 「AはBです」. 私は ミナです (わたしは ミナです) means "I am Mina." If you are a student, you say 「学生です」 (がくせいです), and if you are Korean, 「韓国人です」 (かんこくじんです). です is used in much the same way as the Korean "~입니다" (-imnida).

To ask a question, attach **か** at the end. 「学生ですか」 is "Are you a student?" The answer begins with はい (yes) or いいえ (no). "is not ~" is 「~ではありません」 (or 「~じゃありません」). For example, 「いいえ、学生ではありません」 is "No, I am not a student."

jl-06.title: Reading a Short Text and Writing a Self-Introduction
explain: Let us gather what we have learned so far and read a short text. The text below is a fictional one made specially for this course.
**Reading text**
はじめまして。わたしは ミナです。かんこくじんです。がくせいです。にほんごを べんきょうします。としょかんで ほんを よみます。コーヒーが すきです。どうぞ よろしく おねがいします。

Translated into English it reads: "Nice to meet you. I am Mina. I am Korean. I am a student. I study Japanese. I read books at the library. I like coffee. I look forward to working with you." The new words are as follows.
- かんこくじん: a Korean person
- にほんご: the Japanese language
- べんきょうします: study
- としょかん: library
- ほん: book
- すき: liking. 「コーヒーが すきです」 is "I like coffee," and が is attached to the thing that is liked.

There are three tips for reading. First, divide the sentences at the period (。). Second, find the particles (は, を, で, が) and break the text into chunks. Third, look first at the verb or です at the very end and guess what the sentence is saying.

Written with kanji mixed in, the same text looks like this: 「はじめまして。私はミナです。韓国人です。学生です。日本語を勉強します。図書館で本を読みます。コーヒーが好きです。どうぞよろしくお願いします。」 When kanji are included, the meaning of the words comes at a glance, but you need to know how to read them. At first, a text written only in hiragana is easier to read.

examples.title: Reading a single sentence closely
body: Divided into chunks, 「としょかんで ほんを よみます」 is "at the library / the book (object) / read." で is the place of the action, を is the thing being read, and よみます is the verb. The verb is at the very end.
Just changing a particle changes the meaning. 「としょかんに ほんが あります」 is "There is a book in the library." に and が show the place of existence and the thing that exists.

examples.title: Rewriting it as my own introduction
body: The frame of the text we read is "greeting → name → identity → what I do or what I like → closing greeting." Changing only the words that appear in the text makes it a self-introduction. For example, even if you change the name and change 「コーヒーが すきです」 to another taste, such as "I like tea," the frame stays the same.
If writing in Japanese is hard, you may mix in Korean and Roman letters. What matters is mastering the frame.

jl-07.title: Japanese Giving and Receiving Expressions (あげる, くれる, もらう) and Uchi–Soto Perspective
explain: In Korean, the same verb 'to give' (주다) can be used for both 'I gave my friend a book' and 'my friend gave me a book.' Japanese, however, takes the speaker (me) and the psychological in-group **uchi** (内: family, our side) as the reference point, and strictly distinguishes 'to give' into two different verbs according to the direction in which the object or favor moves.

First, for 'give' in the **centrifugal direction**, moving away from the speaker (uchi) toward other people, the out-group **soto** (外) (in to out, or third party to third party), **あげる** (ageru; the humble, upward form is `さしあげる`, and the downward form is `やる`) is used (for example, `私が友達に本をあげた` 'I gave my friend a book'). Therefore, when another person gives something to the speaker (me) or to my family, `あげる` can never be used, and `*友達が私に本をあげた` is an ungrammatical sentence that violates the perspective constraint.

explain.alt: A table contrasting the verb あげる, for the centrifugal direction from uchi (in-group) to soto (out-group), with the verb くれる, for the centripetal direction from soto to uchi, in Japanese giving and receiving expressions; at the bottom are もらう and the structure of the auxiliary verbs (~てあげる, ~てくれる, ~てもらう).
explain.caption: Differentiation of giving and receiving verbs and auxiliary verbs according to the uchi–soto perspective

explain: Second, for 'give' in the **centripetal direction**, moving closer from soto (another person) toward the speaker (me) or uchi (my family) (outside to inside), **くれる** (kureru; the honorific form is `くださる`) must be used (for example, `友達が私に本をくれた` 'my friend gave me a book' / `友達が妹に本をくれた` 'my friend gave my younger sister a book'). Third, 'receive,' which makes the recipient (the speaker or uchi) the subject, uses **もらう** (morau; the humble form is `いただく`), and the giver is marked with the case particle `に` (or `から`) (`私が友達に本をもらった`).

These three verbs extend, when joined after the `て` form of another verb, into the **giving-and-receiving auxiliary verbs** (`~てあげる`, `~てくれる`, `~てもらう`), which express the direction of gratitude (favor, benefit) for an action. For example, when a friend helped me, taking the friend as the subject gives `友達が手伝ってくれた` ('my friend helped me'), and taking me as the subject gives `(私が)友達に手伝ってもらった` ('I was helped by my friend'), so a single event is always narrated consistently from the speaker's (uchi's) perspective.

The pragmatic limits and cautions are also clear. `~てあげる` ('do for someone') directly shows the benefit the speaker confers on the other person, so saying `荷物を持ってあげましょうか` ('Shall I carry your luggage for you?') to a social superior or someone one is not close to sounds rude. In this case, switching to `お持ちしましょうか` ('Shall I carry it?', a humble expression) is the key norm of Japanese pragmatics.

examples.title: Choosing あげる or くれる as the uchi–soto boundary shifts
body: Sentence A: Mr. Tanaka (out-group) gave my younger brother (uchi) a dictionary. Sentence B: My younger brother (uchi) gave Mr. Tanaka (out-group) a dictionary.

Step 1: A is a centripetal movement from soto (Tanaka) toward the speaker's uchi (younger brother), so it is written `田中さんが弟に辞書をくれた`. Step 2: B is a centrifugal movement from uchi (younger brother) to soto (Tanaka), so it is written `弟が田中さんに辞書をあげた`.
Interpretation: Even if the speaker does not appear in the sentence, if a person close to the speaker (uchi) is the recipient, `くれる` must be chosen.

examples.title: Case particle alternation between ~てくれる and ~てもらう
body: Event: A senior colleague corrected the draft of my paper.
Step 1 (`~てくれる` construction): the agent, the senior colleague, becomes the subject (`が`), giving `先輩が論文を直してくれた` (honorific: `直してくださった`).
Step 2 (`~てもらう` construction): the beneficiary, I, becomes the subject (`は/が`), and the agent, the senior colleague, takes the `に` case, giving `(私は)先輩に論文を直してもらった` (humble: `直していただいた`).

jl-08.title: Voice in Japanese (Passive, Causative, Causative-Passive) and the Syntax of the Adversative Passive
explain: The grammatical category that decides which grammatical case (`が, を, に`) in a sentence the participants in the event shown by the verb (agent, patient, affected party) are placed in is called **voice** (ヴォイス). Japanese voice is systematized around the active as the basic form, with the **passive** (受身), the **causative** (使役), and the **causative-passive** (使役受身), which combines the two.

The biggest syntactic feature of the Japanese **passive** (`-(ら)れる`) is that, unlike in Western languages, two kinds of passive coexist. The first is the **direct passive** (neutral passive), in which the object (`を`) of an active transitive sentence is promoted to the subject (`が/は`) of the passive sentence (for example, `先生が学生をほめた` → `学生が先生にほめられた` 'The student was praised by the teacher'). The second is the **indirect passive** (the adversative passive, **迷惑の受身**), in which a third party (usually the speaker himself or herself) that was not in the original active sentence newly appears as subject and shows that he or she suffered psychological or actual harm because of another person's act or a natural phenomenon.

explain.alt: At the top, the case-particle alternation structure of the four types of Japanese voice (direct passive, indirect adversative passive, causative, causative-passive); at the bottom, a comparison matrix of the modern five-way classification of honorifics (honorific, humble I, humble II, polite and beautifying words).
explain.caption: Argument alternation of voice (passive, causative) and the five-way classification system of honorifics

explain: In the **indirect (adversative) passive**, even an **intransitive verb**, which takes no object, can form a passive sentence. For example, when I was inconvenienced by the event `雨が降った` ('It rained') or `隣でタバコを吸った` ('Someone smoked next to me'), one expresses it as `私は雨に降られた` ('I got rained on and was inconvenienced') or `私は隣の人にタバコを吸われた` ('The person next to me smoked and I suffered for it'). There is also the **possessor passive**, in which a body part or an object belonging to the subject is affected (`私は足を踏まれた` 'I had my foot stepped on'); it keeps the object `足を` as it is and makes the possessor (`私`) the subject.

The **causative** (`-(さ)せる`) is used to make someone perform an action (coercive causative) or to permit or leave something alone (permissive causative). If the original verb is **transitive**, in order to avoid two `を` cases in one sentence (the double-accusative constraint), **`に`** must be attached to the causee (the one performing the action) (`先生が学生に本を読ませた`). On the other hand, if the original verb is **intransitive**, the causee may take `を` (stressing compulsion) or `に` (stressing willingness or permission) (`子供を/に行かせる`). When the passive ending is added to this in turn, the **causative-passive** (`-(さ)せられる`; for Group 1 verbs it may be contracted to `-される`, except for verbs ending in `す`) concentrates the psychology of the victim, 'being forced against one's will to do something' (`私は母に野菜を食べさせられた`).

examples.title: Comparing the number of arguments in the direct passive and the indirect (adversative) passive
body: Sentence A: `泥棒が 私の財布を 盗んだ` ('A thief stole my wallet', converted to a possessor passive). Sentence B: `夜中に 赤ちゃんが 泣いた` ('A baby cried in the middle of the night', converted to an indirect passive).

Step 1: A makes the possessor `私` the subject and leaves the possessed object `財布を`, producing `私は 泥棒に 財布を 盗まれた`. Step 2: B newly adds the victim subject `私` to the intransitive (`泣く`) sentence, producing `私は 夜中に 赤ちゃんに 泣かれた` ('The baby cried and I could not sleep and was troubled').

Interpretation: The key point is that the indirect passive also applies to intransitive verbs, and the total number of arguments (participants) in the sentence increases by one compared with the active sentence.

examples.title: Change in the number of syllables in the contracted causative-passive of Group 1 verbs
body: Compare the basic causative-passive and the contracted causative-passive of the Group 1 (godan) verbs `書く` ('write', stem kak-) and `待つ` ('wait', stem mat-).

Step 1: The basic form is the irrealis stem (`-a`) + `せられる`, so `書かせられる` (6 morae) and `待たせられる` (6 morae). Step 2: In speech `せら` is contracted to the single character `さ`, so `書かされる` (5 morae) and `待たされる` (5 morae) are widely used.
Interpretation: However, a Group 1 verb whose stem ends in `s`, such as `話す` ('speak'), does not use the contracted form (`*話さされる`) and uses only `話させられる`.

jl-09.title: The Five-Way Classification of Japanese Honorifics and the Pragmatics of Addressee Honorifics
explain: Japanese honorifics (敬語 keigo) were traditionally explained in a three-way classification of honorific, humble, and polite language, but since the 2007 report of Japan's Council for Cultural Affairs ("Guidelines for Honorific Language"), academia and education have analyzed them precisely in a **five-way classification of honorifics**, which splits the humble form in two and makes beautifying language independent.

First, **honorific language** (尊敬語) is **subject honorific** language, which raises the agent of the action or state in the sentence (usually the subject). It is realized at three levels: lexical suppletion (`行く/来る/いる` → `いらっしゃる`, `言う` → `おっしゃる`, `食べる/飲む` → `召し上がる`), the grammatical derivational form **`お/ご + verb stem + になる`** (`お読みになる`), and the auxiliary `-(ら)れる`, identical in form to the passive (`先生が来られた`).

Second and third are the two divisions of humble expression, which lowers the action of the speaker (or uchi). **Humble language I** (謙譲語 I) is language that **raises the object (the recipient, direct object, or dative target) toward which the speaker's action is directed, that is, object honorific**, and includes lexical forms (`行く/来る` → `伺う`, `言う` → `申し上げる`, `見る` → `拝見する`) and **`お/ご + stem + する`** (`お荷物をお持ちする`). By contrast, **humble language II** (謙譲語 II, **polite-humble language 丁重語**) is **addressee honorific language that, when the action has no object it is directed toward or there is no need to raise one, merely lowers one's own action formally and politely when addressing the listener**. Typical vocabulary includes `参る` (go/come), `申す` (say), `いたす` (do), and `おる` (be).

Fourth, **polite language** (丁寧語) is addressee honorific language that shows politeness directly to the listener through `です`, `ます`, and `でございます` at the end of the sentence, and fifth, **beautifying language** (美化語) is the expression that attaches `お/ご` before a noun to refine the speaker's own speech, regardless of whom it raises or lowers (`お酒` 'alcohol', `お金` 'money', `ご飯` 'rice, meal').

Pragmatically, the core principle of Japanese honorifics is the system of **relative honorifics** (相対敬語), in contrast to the absolute-honorific tendency of Korean. Within the company one uses honorific language when referring to one's own president (`社長がいらっしゃいました`), but when mentioning one's own company's president to a person from an outside business partner (soto), one must group the president with the speaker's in-group (uchi), drop the title, and lower him with humble language (`佐藤はただいま外出しております` 'Sato is out at the moment'). Grasping this shift of the uchi–soto boundary is the essence of Japanese discourse grammar.

examples.title: Distinguishing humble I (object raising) from humble II (polite language toward the addressee)
body: Situation A: Visiting the home of one's former teacher (`先生の家に伺います`). Situation B: (In an announcement, to the audience) The train will arrive shortly (`まもなく電車が参ります`).

Step 1: The `伺う` of A is humble I, which raises the former teacher (the object), the target of the visit. Step 2: The `参る` of B is humble II (polite-humble language 丁重語), which does not raise a particular object toward which the train is headed but shows formality to the passengers (the addressees) listening to the announcement.

Interpretation: Therefore, even when introducing one's own name for the first time, one does not use `申し上げる`, which raises an object, but humble II, which speaks politely to the addressee, `キムと申します` ('My name is Kim').

examples.title: Converting in-company and out-of-company utterances by the relative honorific principle
body: Event: Our department head (Tanaka) will go to a business partner tomorrow. Utterance 1 (said to a colleague inside the company) vs. utterance 2 (said by phone to a contact at the business partner).
Step 1 (in-company utterance): to the colleague and the speaker, the department head is a superior, so one uses honorific language and says `田中部長が明日いらっしゃいます`.
Step 2 (out-of-company utterance): in front of an outsider (soto), our department head also becomes uchi (in-group), so one uses humble language and lowers him, saying `明日、田中がそちらに伺います(参ります)`.

jl-10.title: Ancient and Heian Verse: The Poetics of Waka in the Man'yōshū and the Kokinshū
explain: In the history of Japanese literature, the native Japanese fixed-form poetry set against Chinese poetry (漢詩) is called **waka** (和歌). Waka takes as its basic rhythm an alternation of 5-mora (syllable) and 7-mora lines, and through the compilation of poetry anthologies in successive eras it formed the framework of classical Japanese aesthetics.

The oldest surviving anthology of waka in Japan is the **Man'yōshū** (万葉集, 20 volumes), compiled in the late eighth century at the end of the Nara period. Since hiragana and katakana had not yet been created, it was recorded in **Man'yōgana** (万葉仮名), which wrote Japanese sounds by borrowing the meaning of Chinese characters (kun reading) or borrowing only their sound (on reading). The **roughly 4,500** poems it contains cover the voices of all social ranks, from emperors and aristocrats (for example, Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, Princess Nukata, and Ōtomo no Yakamochi) to anonymous farmers and border guards (**sakimori** 防人). In verse form, the **chōka** (長歌, 'long poem'), which runs long as `5·7·5·7·…·5·7·7`, coexisted with the **tanka** (短歌, 'short poem') of `5·7·5·7·7` (31 mora), and its core aesthetics were **makoto** (まこと: sincerity, true heart), which expresses unadorned genuine feeling frankly and robustly, and **masuraoburi** (ますらおぶり: a masculine, robust poetic manner).

However, with the spread of hiragana (onnade 女手, 'women's hand') in the Heian (平安) period from the ninth century on, the chōka died out and waka settled completely into the single form of the **tanka of 5·7·5·7·7 (31 mora in total)** (today, 'waka' or 'tanka' refers to this 31-mora form). The **Kokin Wakashū** (古今和歌集, about 1,100 poems), the first **imperially commissioned (勅撰 chokusen: compiled by imperial order) waka anthology**, compiled in 905 by order of Emperor Daigo by **Ki no Tsurayuki** (紀貫之) and others, established **taoyameburi** (たおやめぶり: a feminine, flowing poetic manner), an elegant and refined aesthetic centered on court aristocrats.

In the **Kana Preface** (仮名序) of the Kokinshū, the first full-fledged work of poetic criticism written in Japanese, Ki no Tsurayuki declared that 'waka takes the human heart as its seed and blossoms into the leaves of countless words,' and sang of the changing seasons and the subtle shifts of love. Alongside this, three key rhetorical devices of waka were refined. These are the **makurakotoba** (枕詞, 'pillow word': a fixed epithet of about five mora conventionally placed before a particular word that sets the meter and a classical atmosphere; for example, 'heaven-going' `あまざかる`), the **kakekotoba** (掛詞, 'pivot word': using homophones to overlay two meanings at once on a single run of syllables; for example, overlaying 'pine tree 松' and 'to wait 待つ' on `まつ`), and the **engo** (縁語, 'associated words': placing words associated with the central subject throughout the poem).

Later, the **Shin Kokin Wakashū** (新古今和歌集), the eighth imperial anthology, compiled in 1205 at the end of the Heian and beginning of the Kamakura period by Fujiwara no Teika (藤原定家) and others, opened the aesthetic of medieval lingering resonance through the technique of **honkadori** (本歌取り: allusive variation on an older poem), which restrained the direct exposure of emotion and layered multi-level images by varying phrases of old poems.

examples.title: Calculating the syllable count of a waka (tanka) and the upper-verse/lower-verse structure
body: Analyze the five-line composition (`5 - 7 - 5 - 7 - 7`) of a single 31-mora tanka.

Step 1: The first three lines (`5·7·5`) taken together are called the **upper verse** (上の句 kami no ku, 17 mora), and the last two lines (`7·7`) taken together are called the **lower verse** (下の句 shimo no ku, 14 mora). Step 2: `17 + 14 = 31 mora` is the invariable fixed form of waka (tanka).

Interpretation: The medieval renga (連歌) of later times was born from two people dividing the composition of this upper verse (17 mora) and lower verse (14 mora), and the early modern haiku is the upper verse (17 mora) standing alone.

examples.title: Decoding the 'kakekotoba (掛詞)' in a Kokinshū waka by Ono no Komachi
body: The poem: `花の色は 移りにけりな いたづらに わが身世にふる ながめせしまに` (The color of the flowers has faded, in vain; while I spent my days in the world, gazing in thought at the long rains).

Step 1: In `ふる` (furu), two meanings are overlaid: 'to pass through the world / grow old (経る)' and 'rain falls (降る)'. Step 2: In `ながめ` (nagame), two meanings are overlaid: 'to gaze absently, lost in melancholy (眺め)' and 'long spring rain (長雨)'.

Interpretation: The kakekotoba (掛詞) is a highly sophisticated rhetorical device that, within a short 31 mora, overlays natural scenery (cherry blossoms falling in spring rain) and human affairs (youth withering with the years) at the same time.

jl-11.title: Heian-Period Monogatari and Essays: The Tale of Genji and Mono no Aware
explain: After the dispatch of embassies to Tang China was halted in the late ninth century, Heian (平安, Kyoto) court society brought to flower the **kokufū culture** (国風文化, 'national style culture'), which digested imported Chinese culture with a Japanese sensibility. Male aristocrats of the time were still bound to Chinese (mana 真名, as opposed to kana) in official duties and scholarship, but court women (nyōbo 女房) freely commanded the newly developed phonetic script **hiragana**, opening a golden age of women-led narrative and essay literature that has few parallels in world literary history.

The central genre of Heian prose literature is the **monogatari** (物語: tale literature). The monogatari developed by merging two lines: the **tsukuri monogatari** (作り物語: fictional invented tales) lineage of **The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter** (竹取物語 Taketori Monogatari, the story of Princess Kaguya born inside a bamboo stalk, called the 'ancestor of monogatari'), which began from folk tales, and the **uta monogatari** (歌物語: poem tales) lineage of **The Tales of Ise** (伊勢物語 Ise Monogatari, composed of 125 episodes modeled on Ariwara no Narihira), which strings together the anecdotes behind the composition of waka.

The work that integrated these two traditions and reached the summit of classical narrative literature is **The Tale of Genji** (源氏物語 Genji Monogatari), written in the early eleventh century (around 1008) by the court woman writer **Murasaki Shikibu** (紫式部). This epic novel, with **54 chapters** (帖), about 500 characters, and **795** inserted waka, is broadly structured in three parts. Parts One and Two (the first 41 chapters) depict the splendid glory of the ideal nobleman **Hikaru Genji** (光源氏), his love affairs with many women (Fujitsubo, Murasaki no Ue, and others), and his inner loneliness and fateful sense of guilt. Part Three (the final 13 chapters), which deals with the time after Genji's death (the last 10 chapters in particular are called the **'Uji Ten Chapters'** 宇治十帖 because their main setting is Uji 宇治), centers on Kaoru, Niou no Miya, and Ukifune and probes human salvation and the anguish of renouncing the world with a darker and deeper religious gaze.

Later, the Edo-period scholar of national learning **Motoori Norinaga** (本居宣長) criticized the earlier interpretations that judged The Tale of Genji by Confucian and Buddhist moralizing (rewarding good and punishing evil), and defined the essence of the work as knowing **'mono no aware'** (もののあわれ: the tender sympathy and emotional sigh that spontaneously well up from deep in the heart when one faces the transience and beauty of things and human affairs).

Meanwhile, alongside the monogatari, court women pioneered **diary literature** (日記文学 nikki bungaku: *The Tosa Diary*, the first kana diary, written by Ki no Tsurayuki in the persona of a woman narrator; *The Kagerō Diary* by the mother of Fujiwara no Michitsuna; the diary of Murasaki Shikibu; and *The Sarashina Diary* by the daughter of Sugawara no Takasue), which recorded their autobiographical inner lives, and the **essay** (随筆 zuihitsu). In particular, the essay collection **The Pillow Book** (枕草子 Makura no Sōshi) of **Sei Shōnagon** (清少納言), who served Empress Teishi (定子), realized through some 300 short pieces **'okashi'** (をかし: interesting, a bright and lively charm), an intellectual aesthetic that captures its subject sharply and wittily, forming a vivid pair with Murasaki Shikibu's deepening 'aware' (あわれ) aesthetic.

examples.title: The three-part structure of The Tale of Genji and the narrative shift of the 'Uji Ten Chapters'
body: Compare, among the 54 chapters in all, chapters 1-33 (the glory of youth and middle age), chapters 34-41 (the sorrow of his later years and the death of Murasaki no Ue), and chapters 42-54 (the stories of the descendants after Genji's death, especially chapters 45-54, the 'Uji Ten Chapters').

Step 1: Through chapter 41, the shining life and dark karma of the hero Hikaru Genji intersect against the backdrop of the court in the capital Heiankyō. Step 2: The last ten chapters (the Uji Ten Chapters) take the misty banks of the Uji River, away from the capital, as their main setting and depict the irresolute inner life of the hero Kaoru and the heroine Ukifune's entry into religious life.

Interpretation: This shows that a narrative that began as the life of a single hero deepened, in the later part, into the realm of the modern psychological novel, asking about the loneliness and impermanence of human existence itself.

examples.title: Contrasting Murasaki Shikibu's 'aware' with Sei Shōnagon's 'okashi'
body: Passage A (The Tale of Genji): the transience of life and poignant compassion seeping into the sound of the wind on an autumn evening. Passage B (The Pillow Book, section 1): 'In spring, the dawn (春はあけぼの). The mountain rim growing gradually whiter, brightening little by little, with purplish clouds trailing in thin streaks.'

Step 1: A is 'mono no aware (あわれ)', an aesthetic of emotional absorption and sympathy that wells up from the flow of time and the finitude of human bonds. Step 2: B is 'okashi (をかし)', which captures momentary colors, seasons, and human behavior with clear sensibility and wit.
Interpretation: Heian women's literature perfected, at the same time, two aesthetic axes: lyrical sorrow (aware) and intellectual contemplation (okashi).

jl-12.title: The Turn of Medieval Literature: The Tale of the Heike, Hermit Essays, and Noh Masked Drama with Yūgen
explain: As the Kamakura (鎌倉) shogunate was established at the end of the twelfth century after the civil war between the Taira (平: Heike) and Minamoto (源: Genji) clans, the lead in Japanese literature shifted from Heian court aristocrats to **medieval literature** (the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, late twelfth to late sixteenth century), in which warriors (武士), Buddhist monks and hermits (隠者), and commoners intersected. The core spirit that ran through the age amid war and social change was the Buddhist **view of impermanence** (無常観 mujōkan: the worldview that all glory in the world changes and passes away) and **yūgen** (幽玄: an aesthetic of profound, subtle resonance that is not fully put into words).

The genre representing medieval narrative literature is the **war tale** (軍記物語 gunki monogatari), which takes historical wars as its subject, and its summit is **The Tale of the Heike** (平家物語 Heike Monogatari). This work was completed through the layering of recitation texts (語り本) that blind itinerant performer-monks called **biwa hōshi** (琵琶法師) recited while wandering the country to biwa accompaniment. It is a masterpiece of the **wakan konkōbun** (和漢混淆文, mixed Japanese-Chinese style) that dynamically mixes Chinese-derived vocabulary and native Japanese words, and its famous opening sentence, 'The sound of the bells of the Gion Shōja echoes the impermanence of all things; the color of the sala flowers reveals the truth that the prosperous must decline,' condenses the sudden rise and fall of the Taira clan into heroic beauty of action and Buddhist sorrow.

explain: Meanwhile, in the **hermit literature** (essays) written by intellectuals who withdrew from the world to live in thatched huts, **Hōjōki** (方丈記, 1212) by **Kamo no Chōmei** (鴨長明) (which begins 'The flow of the flowing river never ceases, and yet the water is never the same,' and reflects on a possessionless life in a hut ten feet square amid the disasters of a great fire, an earthquake, and famine) and **Tsurezuregusa** (徒然草, around 1330) by **Yoshida Kenkō** (吉田兼好) (which shows detachment and insight into human nature amid a transient life through 243 essays) completed, together with the Heian *Pillow Book*, the **three great classical Japanese essays**.

By the Muromachi (室町) period, under the patronage of the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the father and son **Kan'ami** (観阿弥) and **Zeami** (世阿弥) brought the traditional performing art sarugaku (猿楽) to fulfillment as **Noh** (能 Nō), an artistic masked song-and-dance drama. In his treatise **Fūshikaden** (風姿花伝, *The Transmission of the Flower of Acting Style*), Zeami defined the actor's vitality as **'hana'** (花: flower, the fresh artistic emotion that captivates the audience) and the ultimate beauty Noh aims at as **'yūgen'** (幽玄: elegant, profound grace). In particular, the **mugen Noh** (夢幻能: dream-phantasm Noh) form, in which the protagonist (**shite** シテ) appears in the first half as an ordinary person and in the second half reveals his true form as a ghost bearing a grudge or attachment from life, and dances and sings to release that sorrow and be saved before a supporting role, a wandering monk (**waki** ワキ), is the crystallization of medieval aesthetics, combining allusions to classical poetry with Buddhist requiem (during the interlude, the realistic colloquial comedy **kyōgen** 狂言 is performed together).

examples.title: Analysis of the parallelism and wakan konkōbun in the opening of The Tale of the Heike
body: The passage: `祇園精舎の鐘の声、諸行無常の響きあり。沙羅双樹の花の色、盛者必衰の理をあらはす` (The sound of the bells of the Gion Shōja has the echo of the impermanence of all things; the color of the sala flowers reveals the truth that the prosperous must decline).

Step 1: It is a 'wakan konkōbun' that combines the solemn Chinese rhythm of four-character expressions in the manner of Chinese poetry (`諸行無常`, `盛者必衰`) with the flowing cadence of native Japanese words (`響きあり`, `理をあらはす`). Step 2: The preceding and following phrases form a perfect parallelism and raise the narrative of the Taira clan's downfall to a universal Buddhist law.

Interpretation: Unlike the delicate kana prose of the Heian period, this is a stylistic innovation that secures at once the dynamism of the warrior age and the musicality of oral recitation literature.

examples.title: Analysis of the dramatic structure of Zeami's 'mugen Noh (夢幻能)'
body: Analyze the order of events in the representative Noh play *Atsumori*.

Step 1 (the first act 前場): When the wandering monk (waki, the former enemy general Kumagai) visits the old battlefield of Ichi-no-tani, a young grass cutter (the maeshite 前シテ) appears, tells of the sound of a flute and old tales, and vanishes. Step 2 (the second act 後場): As the monk chants sutras, the ghost of the armored warrior Atsumori (the nochishite 後シテ) appears in his true form, reenacts his last battle in dance, and washes away his grudge.
Interpretation: The core of mugen Noh is its double structure of time, which summons tragic memory of the past onto the stage of the present to pacify the spirit.

jl-13.title: Edo-Period Townsman Culture, Prose, and Drama: Saikaku and Chikamatsu
explain: The **Edo period** (early modern, 1603-1867), which lasted more than 260 years after Tokugawa Ieyasu opened the shogunate in Edo (Tokyo) in 1603, was a time when warfare ended and the money economy and urban commerce and industry grew by leaps and bounds. Accordingly, the producers and readers of literature also shifted from aristocrats and monks to the urban merchant and artisan class, the **chōnin** (町人 'townspeople'), and with the development of woodblock printing and book-lending shops (kashihon'ya), Japan's first commercial mass-publishing literature was born.

Whereas medieval literature saw this world as a 'world of suffering' (憂き世 ukiyo) and sought salvation in the next, the wealth-accumulating Edo chōnin used a homophone to affirm the present world as the **'floating world'** (浮世 ukiyo: the drifting, sensory reality of the present age, to be enjoyed here and now in its transience). The **Genroku culture** (元禄文化, late seventeenth to early eighteenth century), which first flowered in Kyoto and Osaka (Kamigata 上方), produced realist literature that vividly affirmed basic human desires (love and money).

The figure who revolutionized early modern prose was the Osaka merchant-born writer **Ihara Saikaku** (井原西鶴, 1642-1693). In 1682 he published **The Life of an Amorous Man** (好色一代男 Kōshoku Ichidai Otoko, which depicts the amorous career of the protagonist Yonosuke over his whole life, parodying the 54-chapter structure of *The Tale of Genji*) and thereby founded the genre of manners fiction that depicted the customs of the age realistically, the **ukiyo-zōshi** (浮世草子). Saikaku's literature divides broadly into the **kōshoku-mono** (好色物, 'amorous works': *The Life of an Amorous Man* and *Five Women Who Loved Love*), which deal with human passion and the customs of the pleasure quarters, and the **chōnin-mono** (町人物, 'townsman works': *The Japanese Family Storehouse* and *Worldly Mental Calculations*), which deal with merchants' meticulous money management, bankruptcy, and thrift; with a concise and fast-paced style free of sentiment, he captured the bare face of the early modern city, money and desire.

On the stage, meanwhile, **jōruri** (浄瑠璃, today's **bunraku** 文楽), the puppet theater in which a chanter (tayū 太夫) recites the dialogue and narration to shamisen accompaniment while puppeteers move elaborate puppets, and **kabuki** (歌舞伎), the popular theater of actors, flourished. The playwright **Chikamatsu Monzaemon** (近松門左衛門, 1653-1724), called 'the Shakespeare of Japan,' opened a new horizon of tragedy by pioneering the **sewamono** (世話物, 'domestic plays'), which dealt with real incidents of commoner society of his day, in addition to the **jidaimono** (時代物, historical plays of heroes; for example, *The Battles of Coxinga*).

Chikamatsu's representative sewamono, **The Love Suicides at Sonezaki** (曽根崎心中 Sonezaki Shinjū, 1703) and **The Love Suicides at Amijima** (心中天網島 Shinjū Ten no Amijima, 1720), sublimate into poetic travel scenes (michiyuki 道行) the process by which, when the feudal family system and monetary debts (**giri** 義理: social obligation and honor) collide head-on with individual pure love (**ninjō** 人情: human feeling), a man and woman choose double suicide (shinjū 心中) as their escape from this world. He also left an original theory of theatrical aesthetics holding that art exists neither in complete fiction nor in complete duplication of fact but **'in the thin membrane between the false and the real'** (the kyojitsu hinmaku theory 虚実皮膜論).

Step 1: In medieval Buddhist literature, `憂き世` was the 'sorrowful world' full of pain and impermanence, from which one should escape. Step 2: For Edo chōnin, `浮世` became the 'floating present world,' which, precisely because it is transient, one should affirm and enjoy for its pleasures and reality in this very moment.
Interpretation: This shift of outlook gave birth to ukiyo-zōshi and ukiyo-e (genre woodblock prints), popular arts of the early modern city.

examples.title: The conflict between 'giri (義理)' and 'ninjō (人情)' in Chikamatsu's sewamono tragedies
body: In *The Love Suicides at Sonezaki*, Tokubei, a clerk at a soy sauce shop, is cheated by a friend out of the silver he must return to his master (giri: obligation and credit), and to protect his love (ninjō) for the courtesan Ohatsu, he heads into the woods with her and takes his life.

Step 1: In Edo's feudal commercial society, monetary credit and the honor of one's house (giri) are absolute norms. Step 2: The only paradoxical option that allows one to fulfill one's genuine personal feeling (ninjō) without breaking social norms (giri) is presented as union in the next world (shinjū).
Interpretation: Granting a sublime tragic quality, no less than that of the classical aristocracy, to a nameless lower-class merchant and a courtesan is the innovation of Chikamatsu's sewamono.

jl-14.title: From Early Modern Haikai to Haiku: Matsuo Bashō and Sabi
explain: The 31-mora tanka (5·7·5·7·7) of the Heian period developed in the medieval period into **renga** (連歌), a linked-verse form in which several people gather in one place and compose by alternately linking an upper verse (5·7·5) and a lower verse (7·7). Furthermore, from the late medieval to the early Edo period, **haikai no renga** (俳諧の連歌, abbreviated **haikai** 俳諧), a commoners' linked-verse form that freely allowed everyday colloquial speech and Sino-Japanese words (haigon 俳言) not used in orthodox waka, along with humor and wit, enjoyed whirlwind popularity.

Early haikai (the Teimon and Danrin schools) leaned toward wordplay and comic humor, but in the late seventeenth century **Matsuo Bashō** (松尾芭蕉, 1644-1694) appeared and established the so-called **Shōfū** (蕉風, 'Bashō style') haikai by breathing a high degree of spirituality and contemplation of nature into the **opening verse** (発句 hokku: 17 mora in `5·7·5`), the first verse of haikai. Later, when the Meiji-era literary reformer Masaoka Shiki (正岡子規) named this `5·7·5` short poem, which had become independent of the linked verse, **haiku** (俳句), it came to hold its place as the shortest fixed poetic form in the world today.

For an orthodox haiku to be established, three strict formal rules operate. The first is the fixed form of **5·7·5, 17 mora (syllables) in all**. The second is the rule that within the 17 mora there must be **exactly one** **kigo** (季語, 'season word': a conventional seasonal term, such as 'frog 蛙' and 'cherry blossoms 桜' for spring, 'cicada 蝉' and 'early summer rain 五月雨' for summer, 'autumn leaves' and 'wild geese' for autumn, and 'first snow 初雪' for winter) (a device that evokes, compressed into one word, the vast backdrop of a season). The third is the use of the **kireji** (切れ字, 'cutting word': for example, `や` for exclamation or pause, `かな` for an exclamatory ending, and `けり` for completion or assertion), which cuts the breath of the line and creates tension and blank space between two images.

The core of the haiku aesthetic Bashō pursued is **sabi** (さび 寂: a beauty that, in a desolate and quiet atmosphere after splendor has faded, touches the fundamental solitude of the universe), **shiori** (しおり 撓: a tender resonance that seeps naturally from diction and cadence), and **karumi** (かるみ 軽み: a state he reached in his later years, a charm of shaking off heavy ideas and capturing the ordinary things of daily life lightly and plainly). Bashō also, through the masterpiece of travel literature combining haiku and prose, **The Narrow Road to the Interior** (おくのほそ道 Oku no Hosomichi: 'the path of the heart'; a record of the journey he made in 1689 with his disciple Sora from Edo through the Tōhoku and Hokuriku regions), perfected the pilgrim spirit of fūga (風雅, elegant refinement) expressed in 'the months and days are travelers of eternity.'

In the mid to late eighteenth century, after Bashō's death, **Yosa Buson** (与謝蕪村; 'The spring sea, rolling gently all day long') revived haikai with painterly color and classical romanticism, and in the late Edo period **Kobayashi Issa** (小林一茶) appeared, casting a warm gaze on tiny creatures such as sparrows, frogs, and flies in poor farming villages, so that Bashō, Buson, and Issa are counted as the **three great poets of Edo haiku**.

examples.title: Analysis of the kigo, kireji, and syllable count in Matsuo Bashō's representative poem 'The Old Pond (古池)'
body: The poem: `古池や 蛙飛びこむ 水の音` (`ふるいけや / かわずとびこむ / みずのおと`: the old pond— / a frog jumps in / the sound of water).
Step 1 (syllable count): `ふ・る・い・け・や` (5 mora) + `か・わ・ず・と・び・こ・む` (7 mora) + `み・ず・の・お・と` (5 mora) = 17 mora in total.

Step 2 (kireji and kigo): The `や` at the end of the first line is the **kireji** (cutting word) that cuts the breath and brings the quiet pond into close-up, and `蛙` (frog) is the **kigo** (season word) indicating **spring**. Eternal stillness (the old pond) collides with the momentary dynamic ripple (the sound of water) to produce a deep sense of solitude (sabi).

Interpretation: The form in which this hokku (5·7·5, 17 mora) became completely independent by detaching the lower verse (7·7, 14 mora) is the haiku of the early modern and modern periods.

jl-15.title: Meiji Genbun Itchi, the Modern Novel (Sōseki, Ōgai, the I-Novel), and the Taishō Literary World
explain: The Japanese literary world, which rapidly absorbed modern Western civilization along with the Meiji Restoration (明治維新) of 1868, faced two fundamental tasks. One was the creation of the **genbun itchi** (言文一致, 'unification of spoken and written language') style, which narrates inner life in the actual spoken language, breaking free from the classical literary style and Chinese-influenced diction, and the other was the establishment of a theory of the modern novel that went beyond the premodern gesaku (戯作), light entertainment that preached rewarding good and punishing evil.

In 1885, **Tsubouchi Shōyō** (坪内逍遥), in his critical essay **The Essence of the Novel** (小説神髄 Shōsetsu Shinzui), declared that the core of the novel lies not in moral instruction but in **'the depiction of ninjō (人情: the inner psychology of human beings) and the manners of the age,'** laying the ideological foundation of modern realism. Then **Futabatei Shimei** (二葉亭四迷), in his long novel **Floating Clouds** (浮雲 Ukigumo, 1887-1889), minutely portrayed the inner conflict of the timid intellectual youth Bunzō in genbun itchi prose in the plain `~だ` style, giving birth to the **first modern genbun itchi novel in Japan** (Yamada Bimyō pioneered the `~です` style and Ozaki Kōyō the `~である` style).

explain.alt: A table of the lineage of modern and contemporary Japanese literature: early Meiji genbun itchi (Floating Clouds, The Essence of the Novel); late Meiji naturalism (the I-novel) versus anti-naturalism (Sōseki, Ōgai); late Taishō and early Shōwa (Akutagawa, Kawabata); the postwar period (Dazai, Mishima, Ōe); and on to the present.

explain: In 1906-1907, just after the Russo-Japanese War, it was **naturalism** (自然主義) that dominated the mainstream of the literary world. Shimazaki Tōson's *The Broken Commandment* (1906) raised a social problem, but after **Tayama Katai**'s (田山花袋) **The Futon** (蒲団, 1907: it exposes the ugly inner life of a middle-aged writer who, with the desire he feels for his female pupil, weeps smelling the scent of the bedding she left behind) published the following year, Japanese naturalism turned away from Émile Zola's sociological experimental novel into the uniquely Japanese form of the **I-novel** (私小説 shishōsetsu or watakushi shōsetsu, also called the 'state-of-mind novel'), which confesses the writer's own private life and shameful secrets, without fiction, in something close to the first person.

The two masters who stood against this narrow naturalist and I-novel mainstream and developed intellectual fiction and criticism of civilization were **Natsume Sōseki** (夏目漱石, 1867-1916) and **Mori Ōgai** (森鴎外, 1862-1922). After his early humorous and satirical works (*I Am a Cat* and *Botchan*), Sōseki, in his later trilogy and his masterpiece **Kokoro** (こころ, 1914), deeply probed the **egoism** (selfishness), loneliness, and ethical guilt that the modern intellectual experiences amid rapid Westernization ('externally driven enlightenment'). Mori Ōgai, who studied in Germany as an army surgeon, moved from the early Romantic short story **The Dancing Girl** (舞姫 Maihime, 1890) to later historical fiction ('The Abe Clan') and displayed cool resignation (Resignation) and historical consciousness. Afterward, in the **Taishō** (大正, 1912-1926) literary world, Shiga Naoya (the Shirakaba school) reached the peak of the state-of-mind novel, Tanizaki Jun'ichirō pursued aestheticism, and **Akutagawa Ryūnosuke** (芥川龍之介) sharply dissected human selfishness and the relativity of truth through a short-story aesthetic that reinterpreted classical tales with modern psychology (**Rashōmon** 羅生門, **In a Grove** 藪の中).

examples.title: Comparing Western naturalism and the transformation into the Japanese 'I-novel (私小説)'
body: Contrast nineteenth-century French naturalism (Zola) with the Japanese naturalism (the I-novel) established after Tayama Katai's *The Futon* in 1907.

Step 1: Western naturalism, under the hypothesis that heredity and social environment determine human behavior, objectively observed and experimented on fictional characters and multiple social classes. Step 2: Japanese naturalism equated 'unadorned truth' with 'the defenseless confession of private facts the author personally experienced,' and thus gave rise to the 'I-novel' tradition, which maximized the sincerity of the inner self at the cost of losing social vision.

Interpretation: Afterward, modern and contemporary Japanese literature developed in the tension between the confessional I-novel tradition and the fictional, intellectual novel that sought to overcome it (Sōseki, Akutagawa, and others).

examples.title: The narrative structure of Natsume Sōseki's Kokoro (こころ) and the loneliness of the modern person
body: Kokoro is composed of three parts, 'Sensei and I,' 'My Parents and I,' and 'Sensei and His Testament,' and takes a frame structure in which the narrator 'I' reads the long testament of 'Sensei,' his spiritual teacher.

Step 1: In his university days Sensei betrayed his closest friend K in order to win the daughter of the boarding house, and after K's suicide he lives out his life in guilt and loneliness. Step 2: Hearing the news of the death of the Meiji Emperor and of General Nogi's junshi (following his lord in death), Sensei feels that 'the spirit of Meiji' has ended and takes his own life.
Interpretation: It is a masterpiece that, through an individual's love triangle, captures at once the dark abyss of modern individualism (egoism) and the end of an era.

jl-16.title: The Burai-ha Immediately After the Defeat (Dazai Osamu) and the Aesthetics of Kawabata and Mishima
explain: Japan's defeat in the Pacific War in 1945 and the dismantling of the deification of the emperor (the Humanity Declaration) shook the existing value system of Japanese society to its roots. In the literary world, freed from censorship, there was an intense outburst of literature on the ruins that sought to expose the hypocrisy of the old morality or to reestablish the essence of Japanese beauty.

The current that won the enthusiastic sympathy of the public immediately after the defeat was the **Burai-ha** (無頼派, 'Decadent School' or 'Libertine School,' also called the Shin-gesaku-ha 新戯作派), led by **Dazai Osamu** (太宰治, 1909-1948), Sakaguchi Ango (坂口安吾, essay 'On Decadence'), Oda Sakunosuke, and others. They rejected the wartime militarist ethic and the hypocritical morality of established society, and from the very bottom of self-destruction and decadence sought paradoxically to recover pure humanity. In **The Setting Sun** (斜陽 Shayō, 1947), which depicts a declining aristocratic family, and the posthumously published long novel **No Longer Human** (人間失格 Ningen Shikkaku, 1948), Dazai Osamu poignantly voiced the alienation and existential anxiety of postwar youth through the notebooks of the protagonist **Ōba Yōzō** (大庭葉蔵), who disguises himself with buffoonery (clowning) out of extreme fear of other people and goes to ruin.

By contrast, **Kawabata Yasunari** (川端康成, 1899-1972), who started out in the **Shinkankaku-ha** (新感覚派, 'New Sensation School': which, together with Yokomitsu Riichi, experimented with the sensory style of the Western avant-garde), a strand of early Shōwa modernism, returned deeply to the lyrical traditional beauty of Japanese classics after passing through war and defeat. His masterpieces **Snow Country** (雪国 Yukiguni, 1935-1947 completed: it begins 'The train came out of the long tunnel into the snow country' and depicts the fleeting love between Shimamura and the hot-spring geisha Komako), **Thousand Cranes** (千羽鶴), and **The Sound of the Mountain** (山の音) crystallized into sensuous modern prose the 'mono no aware' of Heian, the 'yūgen' of medieval linked verse, and the aesthetics of blankness and nothingness of Zen Buddhism. For this achievement Kawabata received the **Nobel Prize in Literature in 1968, the first for Japan (the second for Asia)**.

The writer who followed Kawabata and pushed postwar aestheticism and classicist formal beauty to the extreme was **Mishima Yukio** (三島由紀夫, 1925-1970). After *Confessions of a Mask* (1949), a work of autobiographical reflection, Mishima published the masterpiece **The Temple of the Golden Pavilion** (金閣寺 Kinkakuji, 1956), based on the real arson of Kinkaku-ji (the Golden Pavilion) in Kyoto in 1950. In this work, the stuttering young acolyte Mizoguchi tries to move into life at last by burning the Golden Pavilion, the symbol of an absolute beauty that overwhelms his life, and it builds the sharp opposition between beauty and destruction, cognition and action, in an elaborate and ornate artificial style.

The tragic deaths and literary worlds of these three writers (Dazai's drowning in 1948, Mishima's ritual disembowelment in 1970, Kawabata's gas suicide in 1972) symbolically show how fiercely postwar Japanese literature wrestled, in the sense of loss after defeat, with the two extremes of 'the dissolution of the self' and 'the absolutization of traditional aesthetics.'

examples.title: The frame structure and effect of perspective in Dazai Osamu's No Longer Human
body: No Longer Human is composed of a 'Preface' and an 'Afterword,' in which an 'I' who seems to be the author describes three strange photographs, and, placed between them, the protagonist Ōba Yōzō's 'three notebooks.'

Step 1: The main text (the three notebooks) is Yōzō's first-person confession, extremely pouring out the shame and fear within him of failing to adapt to human society and heading toward ruin. Step 2: However, in the final 'Afterword,' the bar madam testifies from a third party's viewpoint about Yōzō, saying 'The Yōzō we knew was a very pure, sensitive child, good as a god.'

Interpretation: By intercutting the inner life of the protagonist who branded himself 'disqualified as a human being' with the testimony of others, it makes three-dimensional that what is truly sick is not Yōzō but the hypocrisy of the world that pushed him out.

examples.title: The sensory compression in the opening of Kawabata Yasunari's Snow Country
body: The passage: `国境の長いトンネルを抜けると雪国であった。夜の底が白くなった。信号所に汽車が止まった` (Coming out of the long tunnel at the border, there was the snow country. The bottom of the night had turned white. The train stopped at a signal stop).

Step 1: It compresses into a single sentence the spatial movement of passing through a dark tunnel (everyday reality, Tokyo) into the pure-white snow country (a space of non-everyday beauty). Step 2: Not 'the night grew bright' but 'the bottom of the night turned white' is a synesthetic and visual expression typical of the Shinkankaku-ha, immediately evoking a cold and quiet atmosphere.
Interpretation: It is the finest example of modern Japanese prose in which the sensory techniques of Western modernism are combined with the haiku-like tradition of omission and blank space.

jl-17.title: Postwar Existentialist and Democratic Literature: Abe Kōbō and Ōe Kenzaburō
explain: In the Japanese literary world after the defeat, a group of writers emerged who sought to think about war responsibility, alienation in the modern city, and existentialist absurdity in the universal language of world literature, going beyond the two poles of the confessional I-novel and traditional lyrical beauty. The representative writers who took up the concerns of the first and second **postwar school** (戦後派 sengoha), such as Ōoka Shōhei (*Fires on the Plain*) and Noma Hiroshi, and widened the horizon of postwar Japanese literature to the world, are **Abe Kōbō** (安部公房, 1924-1993) and **Ōe Kenzaburō** (大江健三郎, 1935-2023).

Abe Kōbō thoroughly excluded Japan's distinctive damp sentiment and the I-novel's everyday life, and pioneered fable-like avant-garde fiction combining the techniques of Franz Kafka with surrealism and existentialism. His representative long novel **The Woman in the Dunes** (砂の女 Suna no Onna, 1962) is the story of the male schoolteacher Niki Jumpei, who, having gone insect collecting, is trapped inside a pit house in a seaside village where sand keeps collapsing endlessly. In the absurd situation of confinement, in which the house would be buried unless the sand is shoveled out every night, the process by which the protagonist moves beyond his obsession with escape, studies the physical properties of sand, and discovers a new existential freedom and identity became a universal allegory that pierces the isolation and repetitive daily life of modern city dwellers (see also *The Face of Another* and *The Box Man*).

Meanwhile, **Ōe Kenzaburō**, standard-bearer of the generation that grew up receiving postwar democratic education, drew on Sartre's existentialism and grotesque realism to deal head-on with the political and ethical tasks of postwar Japan. After his early work **The Catch** (飼育 Shiiku, 1958, winner of the Akutagawa Prize), he reached a literary turning point with **A Personal Matter** (個人的な体験 Kojinteki na Taiken, 1964), which depicts the painful coexistence with and responsibility toward his son born with a congenital brain herniation. The ending, in which the protagonist Bird stops his cowardly flight of trying to abet the disabled child's death and resolves to take on the son's surgery and life head-on, shows the moment when an individual's existential ethics expands into solidarity with others.

Ōe went on to publish **The Silent Cry** (万延元年のフットボール Man'en gannen no Futtobōru, 1967), which gives form to the forest village of his native Shikoku as a mythic cosmos and a peripheral community standing against the emperor-centered power of the state, and *The Game of Contemporaneity*, and through *Hiroshima Notes*, which records the victims of the Hiroshima atomic bombing, and through the problem of Okinawa, he explored throughout his life the postwar pacifist constitution and the salvation of humanity at large. The Swedish Academy highly praised his 'achievement of creating, with poetic force, an imagined world and shockingly depicting the predicament of modern man,' and awarded him the **1994 Nobel Prize in Literature**.

Another important axis of postwar Japanese literature alongside these is **Zainichi Korean literature** (在日文学), which awakened the otherness within the Japanese language, and **contemporary women's literature**. After Kim Dalsu and Kim Seokbeom (whose epic novel *Hwasando* (화산도, 'Volcanic Island') deals with the Jeju 4·3 uprising), **Yi Hoesung** (李恢成, 'The Woman Who Beat the Laundry,' who in 1972 became the first Zainichi Korean to win the Akutagawa Prize) and Yang Sogil, Yu Miri, and Hyeon Wol, who depict the diaspora of later generations, cracked the myth of the single ethnic nation and widened the boundaries of Japanese-language literature. Also, in *Silence* (1966), Endō Shūsaku drew out as a world-class problem work the theological anguish that Western Christianity experiences in collision with the soil of Japan (the 'swamp').

examples.title: Contrasting the Nobel lectures of Kawabata Yasunari (1968) and Ōe Kenzaburō (1994)
body: Compare the titles of the two Japanese Nobel laureates' lectures, 'Japan, the Beautiful, and Myself' (美しい日本の私, Kawabata, 1968) and 'Japan, the Ambiguous, and Myself' (あいまいな日本の私, Ōe, 1994).

Step 1: Kawabata invoked the Zen monk Dōgen, the waka of Saigyō, and the traditional beauty of The Tale of Genji, and presented to the world Japan's distinctive lyrical view of nature and its beauty. Step 2: Ōe deliberately parodied Kawabata's title, critically reflecting that modern Japan is mired in 'ambiguity' amid its history of aggression in Asia and postwar division, and called for ethical solidarity of humanity at large.

Interpretation: The contrast between the two lectures sharply condenses the two great mountain ranges of postwar Japanese literature, 'traditional aestheticism' and 'the postwar democratic spirit of criticism.'

examples.title: Analysis of the spatial symbolism in Abe Kōbō's The Woman in the Dunes
body: Analyze the relationship between the two spaces in the novel, the 'sand pit' and the 'Tokyo apartment and workplace.'

Step 1: At first, to the protagonist the sand pit appears to be an irrational prison cut off from civilized society (Tokyo). Step 2: But as the narrative proceeds, it becomes clear that the daily life of the city, where one's existence is confirmed only by documents and certificates, is the truly sandcastle-like space of alienation.
Interpretation: By erasing the local customs of any specific region of Japan, Abe Kōbō completed an existentialist fable that reads universally to readers of any country.

jl-18.title: Postmodern and Contemporary Japanese Literature and East Asian Comparative Literary Criticism
explain: From the late 1970s and the 1980s, as high economic growth was completed and consumer capitalism and digital informatization became pervasive, Japanese literature broke away from the heavy political and ethical grand narratives of the postwar school and entered the age of **postmodern literature**, which treats the sense of individual loss through a light sensibility and fantastical narrative.

The representative writer who led this shift is **Murakami Haruki** (村上春樹, 1949-). Beginning with his debut *Hear the Wind Sing* (1979), he published **Norwegian Wood** (ノルウェイの森, 1987), **The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle** (ねじまき鳥クロニクル, 1994-1995), *Kafka on the Shore*, *1Q84*, and others, and built a worldwide readership. Haruki abandoned the sticky family relationships and I-novel style of traditional Japanese literature and created a dry, rhythmic, translation-flavored style infused with the sensibility of contemporary American fiction, jazz, and pop culture. In his early work he depicted the gloomy detachment (the **'yare yare'** sentiment) of young people after the Zenkyōtō generation, but with the 1995 Kobe earthquake and the Aum Shinrikyo sarin gas attack on the subway as turning points, he broadened his narrative depth through **'commitment'** to the darkness of the underground world and to historical violence (Manchukuo, the Battle of Nomonhan, and so on).

In the same period, **Yoshimoto Banana** (吉本ばなな), in her novella **Kitchen** (キッチン, 1988), depicted in a clear and transparent style an 'alternative healing community' in which, in the place where the blood-related family has dissolved, strangers tend to one another's sense of loss through the everyday space of the kitchen and shared meals. From the 2000s on, Kawakami Mieko (*Breasts and Eggs*) and Murata Sayaka (*Convenience Store Woman*, 2016: it subversively satirizes the norms of modern society that enforce 'normality' through a protagonist who lives by the convenience-store manual) and others have sharply raised the problems of gender, labor, and non-normative existence.

Further, the most noteworthy current today is **border-crossing literature** (越境文学 ekkyō bungaku, Exophony: literature that goes outside one's mother tongue), which creates in multiple languages beyond the boundaries of the mother tongue (Japanese) and the nation-state. **Tawada Yōko** (多和田葉子, 1960-) writes novels and poems directly in two languages, Japanese and German (*The Suspect's Night Train* and *The Emissary*), and through the gaps between the two languages and the possibility of mistranslation, dismantles the monolingual ideology of 'the national language' (国語 kokugo).

Viewed from the perspective of **East Asian comparative literature**, the crossroads of modern and contemporary Chinese, Japanese, and Korean literature come into sharp focus. The Sino-Japanese coinages that Meiji-era Japan made in translating Western concepts (`literature 文学, society 社会, individual 個人, naturalism 自然主義`) and its experiments with genbun itchi, the I-novel, and the Shinkankaku-ha became directly stimulating and transforming mediators for colonial-era Korea (Yi Gwangsu, Kim Dongin, Yi Sang, and others) and for Chinese students abroad (Lu Xun, Guo Moruo, Yu Dafu, and others). Conversely, today the works of Murakami Haruki, Han Kang, Yu Hua, and others are translated and received among one another around the shared tasks of the loneliness and historical trauma of East Asian urban youth, forming a transnational literary field.

examples.title: The 1995 turning point in Murakami Haruki's narratives (detachment → commitment)
body: Compare the works of the 1980s (*A Wild Sheep Chase*, *Norwegian Wood*) with the works around and after 1995 (*The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle* and the nonfiction *Underground*).

Step 1: The protagonist ('I / boku') of the 1980s works keeps his distance from political and social groups and takes an attitude of 'detachment,' contemplating personal loss. Step 2: Immediately after the 1995 Kobe earthquake and the Aum terrorist attack, Haruki interviewed the victims directly (*Underground*), and in his fiction too he shifted to 'commitment,' engagement with the violence of Japanese imperialism and the structural evil of society.

Interpretation: It shows an ethical leap in which postmodern literature does not remain mere play with consumer culture but confronts the abyss of history (the metaphor of the well and the underground space).

examples.title: Translation and feedback of modern literary concepts in East Asia (a comparative reading)
body: Analyze the relationship that the Chinese writers Lu Xun and Yu Dafu and the Korean writers Yi Gwangsu and Kim Dongin, who were students in Tokyo in the 1900s-1920s, had with the Japanese literary world.

Step 1: While stimulated by Sōseki's satire and by Japanese translations of Andreyev and Gogol, Lu Xun moved, in place of the private confession of the Japanese I-novel, toward a critical realism aimed at the 'spiritual victory method' of the whole nation. Step 2: Yu Dafu and Kim Dongin received the Japanese naturalism and I-novel and the 'modern self' form of the Shirakaba school and laid the foundation of the modern short story in each country.

Interpretation: Comparative literature is not a matter of one-way influence but a discipline that clarifies how the receiver independently refracted and recreated an imported form to fit his or her own historical conditions.
