jl-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Analysis of Japanese Perspective, Voice, and Honorific Discourse and Synthesis of Classical Verse Meter
explain: In the first capstone lesson of the Japanese language and literature bachelor's program, we integrate the analytical tools of **Japanese linguistics** studied in stages 2-5 (uchi–soto perspective, giving and receiving expressions, the passive, causative, and causative-passive, the five-way classification of honorifics and relative honorifics) and **Japanese literature** (the syllable-count meter of waka, renga, and haiku, and the history of classical and modern aesthetics) to read actual discourse and literary texts across both fields.

First is the **integrated grammatical operation of the uchi–soto (内·外) perspective**. A Japanese sentence does not stop at stating a single proposition; it obligatorily marks, with grammatical morphemes, from what position the speaker views the event. (1) In giving and receiving expressions, it forces `くれる/くださる` when the direction of movement is outside to inside, and `あげる/さしあげる` when inside to outside. (2) In voice (ヴォイス), it captures the psychological effect an external event has had on the speaker (uchi) through the **indirect (adversative) passive** (`雨に降られた`), which passivizes even intransitive verbs. (3) In honorifics, it operates the **relative honorific** rule that lowers the actions of one's own company's superior (uchi) with **humble language** (`おります, 参ります`) in front of outsiders (soto). That is, giving and receiving, voice, and honorifics are all threaded together by the single principle of the speaker's perspective in concentric circles (uchi–soto).

Second is the **morphological and syntactic decoding of complex predicate constructions**. In actual Japanese literary texts and advanced discourse, `verb stem + causative + passive + giving-receiving auxiliary + honorific` are chained together (for example, `読まされた`, `書いていただいた`, `お持ちしましょうか`). Here one must trace back the process of alternation of the case particles (`が, に, を`) that each suffix and auxiliary verb requires, in order to decode exactly who is the agent and who is the beneficiary or victim.

Third is the **quantitative and structural reading of the syllable-count meter of classical and early modern fixed-form poetry and the aesthetics of each period**. The history of Japanese verse developed on the combinatory rule of 5 and 7 mora. The **tanka (waka)** of the ancient and Heian periods sang `makoto` and `mono no aware` by planting makurakotoba and kakekotoba within `5·7·5·7·7` (31 mora), and, passing through the medieval **renga**, the early modern Edo **haiku** made the opening verse (hokku) `5·7·5` (17 mora) independent and opened the universe of `sabi` (the beauty of desolation) with only a single season word (**kigo**) and cutting word (**kireji**).

Through the examples and the comprehensive questions below, complete the correction of discourse errors, the inference of argument case particles, the calculation of mora counts of fixed-form poetry, and the reading of literary-historical lineages.

examples.title: Correcting a compound error of perspective, giving-receiving, and relative honorifics in an external phone conversation
body: Erroneous utterance (a company employee speaking to Mr. Sato of a business partner): `*佐藤様、うちの田中部長が 資料を 送ってあげましたか。`

Step 1 (perspective and giving-receiving error): Using `~てあげる` for the act of sending from one's own company (uchi) to the business-partner party (soto) becomes a rude expression that flaunts a favor conferred, and attaching the title `部長` to one's own company's superior is also a violation of relative honorifics.

Step 2 (correct revision): Lower one's own company's superior to `田中`, and using humble language I (`お送りする`), which raises the other party (the object), revise it to `佐藤様、弊社の田中が資料をお送りしましたでしょうか(お届けいたしましたでしょうか)`.

examples.title: Cross-verification of the syllable meter and rhetoric of waka (31 mora) and haiku (17 mora)
body: Compare the total mora count of two tanka (31 × 2 = 62 mora) with the total mora count of three haiku (17 × 3 = 51 mora) and contrast the essential devices of each.
Step 1: One tanka is upper verse (17 mora) + lower verse (14 mora) = 31 mora, and the kakekotoba (掛詞), which overlays homophones, is the key rhetorical device.
Step 2: One haiku is 5·7·5 = 17 mora, and one kigo (季語) indicating the season and the kireji (切れ字: `や, かな, けり`) that cuts the breath are the key devices.

jl-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: An Integrated Critique of the Aesthetics, Narrative, and Comparative Literature of Japanese Literary Texts
explain: The final capstone task of Lesson 20 is to select one key text (or texts from two eras) from classical and early modern Japanese literature or modern and contemporary literature and to complete a bachelor's-level critical essay that combines **(1) the characteristics of Japanese style, orthography, and discourse grammar, (2) the genre form and aesthetic ideal, and (3) the historical context and comparative-literary significance**.

The core of Japanese literary criticism lies in arguing for a work's theme within **the changes of the linguistic medium and of aesthetic concepts**. For example, if you take up a classical or early modern text, you must analyze how the development of hiragana (onnade) made possible the delicate inner depiction and **'mono no aware'** of The Tale of Genji, how wakan konkōbun and biwa recitation made the **'view of impermanence'** of The Tale of the Heike resound, or how the extreme compression of 17 mora (kigo and kireji) created the **'sabi'** of Bashō's haiku.

The same holds when treating modern and contemporary texts. If you analyze Futabatei Shimei and Natsume Sōseki (*Kokoro*), you must show how the **genbun itchi** style and frame narrative dissected the loneliness and egoism of the modern individual, and if you treat Tayama Katai (*The Futon*) or Dazai Osamu (*No Longer Human*), you must point out how Japan's distinctive **I-novel** (私小説) tradition and the first-person confessional form operate. Also, when criticizing Kawabata Yasunari (*Snow Country*), Ōe Kenzaburō, Abe Kōbō (*The Woman in the Dunes*), Murakami Haruki, and Tawada Yōko, you can cross the inheritance of traditional aesthetics with existential and postmodern subversion, and further with an East Asian comparative-literary perspective.

It is recommended that the critical essay be organized with the following five subheadings. **[1. Definition of the text under analysis and its period and genre] → [2. Analysis of style, perspective, and formal devices] → [3. Core aesthetic ideals and themes] → [4. Literary-historical position and diachronic/comparative-literary contrast] → [5. Contemporary reflection and critical conclusion]**. This task is not graded automatically, and after submitting it you check your own essay yourself with the checklist.

examples.title: An example of an integrated critique design: comparing the aesthetic lineage of The Tale of Genji and Kawabata's Snow Country
body: Topic: A comparison of the 'mono no aware' of the Heian classic and the lyricism of the modernist novel Snow Country.

Step 1 (analysis of language and form): The Tale of Genji depicted the transience of human bonds through its long hiragana sentences and the exchange of 795 waka, whereas Kawabata's Snow Country employed the compressed, synesthetic modern style of the Shinkankaku-ha and a haiku-like technique of omission.

Step 2 (aesthetic and comparative evaluation): Both works share a pathos for beauty that vanishes in time (mono no aware), but, as Ōe Kenzaburō pointed out, one can also critically reflect together on the danger that such traditional aestheticism erases historical and social otherness.
